y-m-41-01.title: Can the rule 'if a product is 0, one factor is 0' be used for matrices too?
y-m-41-01.topic: When the product of two matrices that are not zero matrices becomes a zero matrix
y-m-41-01.goal: Judge with a counterexample whether the rule 'if a product is 0, one factor is 0', which held for numbers, also holds for matrices, and consider how the conclusion changes when you switch to a different matrix.
y-m-41-01.material: For real numbers a, b, if ab=0 then a=0 or b=0. Jian thought this rule could be used for matrices too and said this: "If AB=O and A is not a zero matrix, then B is a zero matrix." Here O is the 2×2 zero matrix with all entries 0. A is a 2×2 matrix whose first row is (1, 2) and second row is (2, 4), and B is a 2×2 matrix whose first row is (p, q) and second row is (r, s). All the entries are integers.
y-m-41-01.thinking.0: Judge whether a rule for numbers can be carried over to matrices as it is
y-m-41-01.thinking.1: Make a counterexample that satisfies the condition directly
y-m-41-01.thinking.2: Tell apart matrices where a counterexample arises and matrices where it does not
y-m-41-01.prereq.0: The H1 label is only a difficulty and support tier for this production assignment, not a grade set by the curriculum. It assumes students who have already studied matrices at an introductory high school level.
y-m-41-01.prereq.1: You can calculate the product of 2×2 matrices using entries
y-m-41-01.prereq.2: Know the meaning of an inverse matrix (a matrix that gives the identity matrix E when multiplied)
y-m-41-01.s.s1.prompt: You want to find out whether Jian's claim is right. What is the most suitable first step?
y-m-41-01.s.s1.hint.0: Write in a sentence what kind of B you need to have just one of to break the claim.
y-m-41-01.s.s1.hint.1: Write one entry of AB using p, q, r, s, and find one case where it becomes 0.
y-m-41-01.s.s1.o.a: Since A is not a zero matrix, accept that B is a zero matrix, as with numbers
y-m-41-01.s.s1.r.a: You carried the rule used for numbers over to matrices as it is. Write down directly what must hold for the sums of products of entries for the product to be O.
y-m-41-01.s.s1.o.b: You cannot make any judgment before knowing all the entries of B
y-m-41-01.s.s1.r.b: Even without deciding B, you can judge if there is just one B that breaks the claim. Recall how a 'claim about all B' is tested.
y-m-41-01.s.s1.o.c: Test whether, among B that are not zero matrices, there is one with AB=O
y-m-41-01.s.s1.r.c: You saw that the claim is about 'all B' and set your direction toward finding an example that fits the condition.
y-m-41-01.s.s1.o.d: Since the entries of A have no negative numbers, the entries of AB cannot be 0
y-m-41-01.s.s1.r.d: Even if A has no negative numbers, if entries of B are negative, the sum of products can be 0. Think widely about the possible values of B.
y-m-41-01.s.s1.explain: A claim that 'it holds for all B' is broken by a single B that satisfies the condition while the conclusion is wrong. So finding and testing a B that is not a zero matrix with AB=O is the suitable first step.
y-m-41-01.s.s2.prompt: Make two different B that are not zero matrices with AB=O. The entries p, q, r, s are integers from −9 to 9.
y-m-41-01.s.s2.hint.0: Write the four entries of AB directly using p, q, r, s, and write what is needed for all of them to be 0.
y-m-41-01.s.s2.hint.1: Compare whether the same condition repeats among the formulas you wrote.
y-m-41-01.s.s2.ok.c1: The entries are integers from −9 to 9.
y-m-41-01.s.s2.fail.c1: The entries must be integers from −9 to 9.
y-m-41-01.s.s2.ok.c2: B is not a zero matrix.
y-m-41-01.s.s2.fail.c2: B is a zero matrix. At least one of the entries must not be 0.
y-m-41-01.s.s2.fail.c3: Row 1, column 1 of AB (1×p+2×r) is not 0.
y-m-41-01.s.s2.fail.c4: Row 1, column 2 of AB (1×q+2×s) is not 0.
y-m-41-01.s.s2.explain: The first row of AB is (p+2r, q+2s) and the second row is (2p+4r, 2q+4s). The second row is 2 times the first row, so if p+2r=0 and q+2s=0, then AB=O. For example, if the first row of B is (2, 0) and the second row is (−1, 0), neither A nor B is a zero matrix but AB=O.
y-m-41-01.s.s2.because.prompt: Pick one B you found, show that all the entries of AB are 0, and write what you learned about Jian's claim.
y-m-41-01.s.s2.because.hint.0: If you calculate only row 1, column 1 and row 1, column 2 of AB, look at what happens to the other entries.
y-m-41-01.s.s2.because.hint.1: Use both 'A is not a zero matrix' and 'B is not a zero matrix' and finish the conclusion in one sentence.
y-m-41-01.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: With the B you chose, did you actually calculate and show that all four entries of AB are 0?
y-m-41-01.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you clearly say that neither A nor B is a zero matrix?
y-m-41-01.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Did you write knowing that one example is enough to break a claim about 'all B'?
y-m-41-01.s.s2.because.model.0: If the first row of B is (2, 0) and the second row is (−1, 0), all entries of AB are 0, so AB=O. Neither A nor B is a zero matrix but the product is a zero matrix, so the rule for numbers that if a product is 0, one factor is 0 does not hold for matrices.
y-m-41-01.s.s2.because.model.1: If you take p=0, q=2, r=0, s=−1, AB is the zero matrix with all entries 0. The product can be a zero matrix even when neither is a zero matrix, so Jian's statement was wrong.
y-m-41-01.s.s3.prompt: Jian said again, "That's because the two rows of A are multiples of each other." If you use A′ (first row (1, 2), second row (3, 4)) instead of A, can A′B=O happen for a B that is not a zero matrix? (A′ has an inverse matrix. This is because 1×4−2×3=−2 is not 0.)
y-m-41-01.s.s3.hint.0: Write what would change if you multiply both sides of the equation A′B=O by a matrix related to A′.
y-m-41-01.s.s3.hint.1: Compare how the difference between A and A′ (whether there is an inverse matrix) affects finding a B with AB=O.
y-m-41-01.s.s3.o.a: It cannot happen. Multiplying both sides of A′B=O by the inverse matrix of A′ gives B=O
y-m-41-01.s.s3.r.a: You judged the situation with the changed condition by using the new property of A′ (it has an inverse matrix).
y-m-41-01.s.s3.o.b: It can happen. The product of two matrices that are not zero matrices can be O in any case
y-m-41-01.s.s3.r.b: You extended the conclusion from the earlier example to all A. Look again at which property of A was used in that example.
y-m-41-01.s.s3.o.c: I tested a few B and none seemed to give O, so it cannot happen
y-m-41-01.s.s3.r.c: Testing raises confidence, but it does not check all B. Think about whether there is a way to reason about all B at once.
y-m-41-01.s.s3.o.d: It can happen. The entries of A′ are larger than those of A, so there is more room for the product to be 0
y-m-41-01.s.s3.r.d: The size of entries is not a criterion for judging. Work out how the fact that there is an inverse matrix connects to the equation AB=O.
y-m-41-01.s.s3.explain: If A′ has an inverse matrix, you can multiply both sides of A′B=O by that inverse to get B=O. So a B that is not a zero matrix cannot satisfy A′B=O. The earlier A had no inverse matrix, so this conclusion did not follow.
y-m-41-01.s.s3.acc.0: Testing several B and raising your confidence is a reasonable start. However, you cannot check every B, so reasoning about all B at once with a property like an inverse matrix is more certain.

y-m-41-02.title: The solution 'AB=AC, so B=C': where did it go wrong?
y-m-41-02.topic: Conditions under which you may conclude B=C from AB=AC
y-m-41-02.goal: Find the line in a matrix solution that used a property of numbers without grounds, work out the condition that makes the conclusion correct, and make a counterexample directly for when that condition is missing.
y-m-41-02.material: A, B, C are all 2×2 matrices and O is the zero matrix with all entries 0. Jiho solved as below and concluded "If AB=AC, then B=C."
y-m-41-02.thinking.0: Check which property each line of the solution relies on
y-m-41-02.thinking.1: Find the condition needed for the conclusion to hold
y-m-41-02.thinking.2: Make a counterexample for the case without the condition
y-m-41-02.prereq.0: The H1 label is only a difficulty and support tier for this production assignment, not a grade set by the curriculum. It assumes students who have already studied matrices at an introductory high school level.
y-m-41-02.prereq.1: You can check addition, multiplication, and the distributive law of 2×2 matrices using entries
y-m-41-02.prereq.2: Know the meaning of an inverse matrix (a matrix that gives the identity matrix E when multiplied)
y-m-41-02.s.s1.prompt: Choose the line in Jiho's solution whose grounds are not right.
y-m-41-02.s.s1.hint.0: Next to each line, write what property was used to get that line from the previous line.
y-m-41-02.s.s1.hint.1: For a line where it is hard to give grounds, plug in one specific 2×2 matrix and test whether it really works out that way.
y-m-41-02.s.s1.line.1: Subtracting AC from both sides gives AB−AC=O.
y-m-41-02.s.s1.line.2: Factoring by the distributive law gives A(B−C)=O.
y-m-41-02.s.s1.line.3: A is not a zero matrix, so dividing both sides by A gives B−C=O.
y-m-41-02.s.s1.explain: It is line 4. Up to line 3, the equations come from properties of equality and the distributive law. But line 4 'divided' by A only because A is not a zero matrix. For matrices, even when A is not a zero matrix, it can be that A(B−C)=O while B−C is not a zero matrix. For example, if both rows of A are (1, 1) and the first row of B−C is (1, −1) and the second row is (−1, 1), then A(B−C)=O.
y-m-41-02.s.s2.prompt: For Jiho's conclusion B=C to be right, what more must be known about A so that the grounds for line 4 can be fixed?
y-m-41-02.s.s2.hint.0: First say by what property line 4 is justified in the multiplication of numbers.
y-m-41-02.s.s2.hint.1: Put the condition of each option into A with all entries 1 (a matrix whose two rows are the same) and check whether that A satisfies the condition.
y-m-41-02.s.s2.o.a: All entries of A are positive. There is no entry that is 0 or negative
y-m-41-02.s.s2.r.a: Even if all entries are positive, for an A whose two rows are the same (for example, all entries 1), there can be a B−C that is not a zero matrix with A(B−C)=O.
y-m-41-02.s.s2.o.b: A has an inverse matrix (there exists a matrix that gives E when multiplied)
y-m-41-02.s.s2.r.b: You noticed the condition under which 'dividing' can be turned into multiplying by an inverse matrix.
y-m-41-02.s.s2.o.c: A is symmetric. The entry at row 1, column 2 and the entry at row 2, column 1 are equal
y-m-41-02.s.s2.r.c: Even if it is symmetric, the same counterexample arises with the A that has all entries 1. Test how the symmetric shape is related to cancelling.
y-m-41-02.s.s2.o.d: B and C are both not zero matrices
y-m-41-02.s.s2.r.d: A condition on B and C has nothing to do with dividing by A. Look again at how the line that must be fixed relates to A.
y-m-41-02.s.s2.explain: If A has an inverse matrix, you can multiply both sides of A(B−C)=O by that inverse to get B−C=O. The conditions that all entries are positive or that it is symmetric cannot justify this step.
y-m-41-02.s.s3.prompt: Say that both rows of A are (1, 1), and the first row of B is (1, 2) and the second row is (3, 4). Make one C that is different from B and has AB=AC, and confirm it with the results of calculating AB and AC.
y-m-41-02.s.s3.hint.0: First observe how each entry of AC changes as you change a few entries of C.
y-m-41-02.s.s3.hint.1: Calculate the four entries of AB first, and find a C whose AC entries become equal to them.
y-m-41-02.s.s3.placeholder: Example: If the first row of C is (…, …) and the second row is (…, …), then ...
y-m-41-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Is the C you made really a different matrix from B?
y-m-41-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you calculate each entry of AC directly and compare with AB?
y-m-41-02.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you think about how this example connects to why the 'dividing' on line 4 is not allowed?
y-m-41-02.s.s3.model.0: If the first row of C is (0, 3) and the second row is (4, 3), it differs from B. The first row of AC is (0+4, 3+3)=(4, 6) and the second row is also (4, 6), and both rows of AB are also (4, 6), so AB=AC but B≠C.
y-m-41-02.s.s3.model.1: If you take C with first row (2, 1) and second row (2, 5), it is a different matrix from B. But both rows of AC are (2+2, 1+5)=(4, 6) and both rows of AB are (1+3, 2+4)=(4, 6), so AB=AC.

y-m-41-03.title: Designing roads between two towns to hit a number of routes
y-m-41-03.topic: Writing a one-way road network as a matrix and working out the number of routes that use two roads
y-m-41-03.goal: Understand that an entry of a matrix product means 'the number of routes that use two roads', and build several different road designs that satisfy many conditions at the same time.
y-m-41-03.material: There are two towns, X and Y, and all roads are one-way. In the matrix R, the entry a at row 1, column 1 is the number of loop roads that start at X and return to X, b at row 1, column 2 is the number of roads from X to Y, c at row 2, column 1 is the number of roads from Y to X, and d at row 2, column 2 is the number of loop roads that start at Y and return to Y. Each number of roads is an integer from 0 to 3. A route goes along two roads in order, and if even one road it uses is different, it counts as a different route. Routes that use the same loop road twice are also counted.
y-m-41-03.thinking.0: Interpret what the entries of a matrix product count
y-m-41-03.thinking.1: Build a design that satisfies several conditions at the same time
y-m-41-03.thinking.2: Compare different designs without sticking to a single answer
y-m-41-03.prereq.0: The H1 label is only a difficulty and support tier for this production assignment, not a grade set by the curriculum. It assumes students who have already studied matrices at an introductory high school level.
y-m-41-03.prereq.1: You can calculate the product of 2×2 matrices (pair up the entries of rows and columns, multiply, and add)
y-m-41-03.prereq.2: Know that squaring a matrix means multiplying the same matrix twice
y-m-41-03.s.s1.prompt: The entry at row 1, column 2 of R², the square of the matrix R, is ab+bd. What does this number count?
y-m-41-03.s.s1.hint.0: First write in words what each of a, b, c, d counts.
y-m-41-03.s.s1.hint.1: Write out ab and bd each as 'which road after which road, going from which town to which town'.
y-m-41-03.s.s1.o.a: The number of routes that start at X and arrive at Y using only one road
y-m-41-03.s.s1.r.a: The number of ways to go from X to Y by one road is b itself, at row 1, column 2 of R. Think about what it means that numbers are multiplied.
y-m-41-03.s.s1.o.b: The number of round-trip routes that go from X to Y and come back to X
y-m-41-03.s.s1.r.b: For a round trip, the arrival town must be X. Check what the position row 1, column 2 says about the start and the arrival.
y-m-41-03.s.s1.o.c: The number of routes that start at X and arrive without passing through Y even once
y-m-41-03.s.s1.r.c: One of the two terms of ab+bd uses the loop road d at Y, and the arrival is Y. Work out which town each term passes through.
y-m-41-03.s.s1.o.d: The number of routes that start at X and arrive at Y by using two roads
y-m-41-03.s.s1.r.d: You interpreted the way entries are paired in a product as 'attaching a second road'.
y-m-41-03.s.s1.explain: In ab+bd at row 1, column 2 of R², ab is the number of routes X→X→Y (a loop road, then X→Y) and bd is the number of routes X→Y→Y (X→Y, then a loop road). It counts the routes that go from X and arrive at Y by using exactly two roads in order.
y-m-41-03.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different road designs (a, b, c, d) that satisfy all three of the following. (1) The routes that start at X and arrive at Y using exactly two roads number exactly 3. (2) The routes that start at Y and arrive at X using exactly two roads number at least 1. (3) There are at most 5 roads in total.
y-m-41-03.s.s2.hint.0: Write the number of routes in (1) directly as a formula in a, b, d, and check one by one the combinations of values that give 3.
y-m-41-03.s.s2.hint.1: When you find one, check (2) and (3), and if it does not fit, change it a little at a time, for example by swapping a and d.
y-m-41-03.s.s2.var.a: a (number of loop roads at X)
y-m-41-03.s.s2.var.b: b (number of roads from X to Y)
y-m-41-03.s.s2.var.c: c (number of roads from Y to X)
y-m-41-03.s.s2.var.d: d (number of loop roads at Y)
y-m-41-03.s.s2.ok.c1: The numbers of roads are integers from 0 to 3.
y-m-41-03.s.s2.fail.c1: The numbers of roads must be integers from 0 to 3.
y-m-41-03.s.s2.ok.c2: There are 3 routes from X to Y using two roads.
y-m-41-03.s.s2.fail.c2: The routes from X to Y using two roads (ab+bd) do not number 3.
y-m-41-03.s.s2.ok.c3: There are routes from Y to X using two roads.
y-m-41-03.s.s2.fail.c3: There are no routes from Y to X using two roads (ca+dc).
y-m-41-03.s.s2.ok.c4: There are at most 5 roads in total.
y-m-41-03.s.s2.explain: (1) is ab+bd=b(a+d)=3, so (b, a+d)=(1, 3) or (3, 1). (2) is the condition c(a+d)≥1 and (3) is the condition a+b+c+d≤5. Many designs, such as (a, b, c, d)=(1, 1, 1, 2), (0, 1, 1, 3), (3, 1, 1, 0), (2, 1, 1, 1), all satisfy the conditions. (1, 3, 0, 0) has no route from Y to X, and (3, 1, 2, 0) has 6 roads, so they do not work.
y-m-41-03.s.s3.prompt: Pick one design you made, write all the routes that start at X and arrive at Y using two roads, and write why there are 3.
y-m-41-03.s.s3.hint.0: Split into cases according to which road starting from X is passed first, and write them out.
y-m-41-03.s.s3.hint.1: In each case, count how many roads can be passed second, multiply, and then add.
y-m-41-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you split and count the routes starting from X without missing any, according to where the first road goes?
y-m-41-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say where the product (number of roads × number of roads) and the sum (adding the cases) each come from?
y-m-41-03.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you not leave out the routes that pass through a loop road?
y-m-41-03.s.s3.model.0: For (a, b, c, d)=(1, 1, 1, 2), there is 1×1=1 route X→X→Y through the loop road at X, and X→Y→Y, going X→Y and then through a loop road at Y, is 1×2=2, so there are 3 routes in all.
y-m-41-03.s.s3.model.1: For (0, 1, 1, 3), X has no loop road, so X→X→Y is 0 routes, and the routes that go X→Y and then through one of the 3 loop roads at Y number 1×3=3, so there are 3 routes in all.

y-m-41-04.title: Can we find the prices from the sales records of two days?
y-m-41-04.topic: Judging whether the information is sufficient in a system of linear equations written with matrices
y-m-41-04.goal: Learn that in a system of linear equations written with matrices, two records may still not fix the prices to one value, and design what extra information would fix them.
y-m-41-04.material: A snack shop wrote down its daily sales counts and total sales. On Monday it sold 2 rolls of gimbap and 3 bowls of ramyeon for 13000원, and on Tuesday it sold 4 rolls of gimbap and 6 bowls of ramyeon for 26000원. Prices are the same regardless of the day: one roll of gimbap is x원 and one bowl of ramyeon is y원, and both are positive integers in units of 100원. Written with matrices, the result of multiplying the matrix with first row (2, 3) and second row (4, 6) by (x, y) is (13000, 26000).
y-m-41-04.thinking.0: Judge that the number of equations and the amount of information may not be the same
y-m-41-04.thinking.1: Design what to fill in the missing information with
y-m-41-04.thinking.2: Tell apart information that overlaps with the new information
y-m-41-04.prereq.0: The H1 label is only a difficulty and support tier for this production assignment, not a grade set by the curriculum. It assumes students who have already studied matrices at an introductory high school level.
y-m-41-04.prereq.1: You can calculate the product of a 2×2 matrix and a column vector
y-m-41-04.prereq.2: Know what a system of equations made of two linear equations is
y-m-41-04.s.s1.prompt: Can x and y be fixed to one value with just these two records?
y-m-41-04.s.s1.hint.0: Put the numbers of Monday's record and the numbers of Tuesday's record side by side and compare.
y-m-41-04.s.s1.hint.1: Test whether you can find two different pairs (x, y) that fit both records.
y-m-41-04.s.s1.o.a: They can be fixed. Because there are two equations and two unknown prices
y-m-41-04.s.s1.r.a: This judgment only counted the number of equations. Compare whether the two equations give different information.
y-m-41-04.s.s1.o.b: They cannot be fixed. Tuesday's record is 2 times Monday's, so there is no new information
y-m-41-04.s.s1.r.b: You looked at the relation between the two records and judged that the information overlaps.
y-m-41-04.s.s1.o.c: They cannot be fixed. Because we do not know which of gimbap and ramyeon is more expensive
y-m-41-04.s.s1.r.c: The conclusion is the same but the reason is different. Test whether the prices would be fixed to one value even if we knew which is more expensive.
y-m-41-04.s.s1.o.d: They can be fixed. Because gimbap 2000원 and ramyeon 3000원 fit both records
y-m-41-04.s.s1.r.d: Finding one pair that fits both records is a good test. But check whether gimbap 5000원 and ramyeon 1000원 also fit both records.
y-m-41-04.s.s1.explain: Tuesday's record (4 rolls, 6 bowls, 26000원) is exactly 2 times Monday's record (2 rolls, 3 bowls, 13000원), so it gives no new information. There are many pairs (x, y) that fit both records, such as (2000, 3000) and (5000, 1000), so they cannot be fixed to one.
y-m-41-04.s.s2.prompt: You want to write down the sales counts and total sales on Wednesday too, and fix x and y to one value using the Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday records. If you sell u rolls of gimbap and v bowls of ramyeon on Wednesday, is it possible? Make 3 different possible (u, v). (u and v are integers from 0 to 9, and Wednesday's total sales are written to match the real prices.)
y-m-41-04.s.s2.hint.0: Write one case where Wednesday's (u, v) has the same ratio as Monday's (2, 3) and one case where it has a different ratio.
y-m-41-04.s.s2.hint.1: Compare whether the two equations made from Monday's (2, 3) and Wednesday's (u, v) give different information.
y-m-41-04.s.s2.ok.c1: u and v are integers from 0 to 9.
y-m-41-04.s.s2.fail.c1: u and v must be integers from 0 to 9.
y-m-41-04.s.s2.ok.c2: Wednesday's sales have a different ratio from Monday's, so they become new information.
y-m-41-04.s.s2.fail.c2: Wednesday's sales have the same ratio as Monday's (or it is a day when nothing was sold), so they cannot become new information.
y-m-41-04.s.s2.explain: Monday's sales ratio is gimbap 2 : ramyeon 3. If Wednesday's (u, v) differs from this ratio (that is, if 2v−3u is not 0), the two equations give different information and x and y are fixed to one value. A case with the same ratio such as (2, 3) or (4, 6), or (0, 0) where nothing was sold, does not add information.
y-m-41-04.s.s2.because.prompt: In one or two sentences, write what difference there is between (u, v) that fix the prices and (u, v) that do not, compared with Monday's record.
y-m-41-04.s.s2.because.hint.0: Write (2, 3) and (4, 6) as equations and check whether one equation immediately gives the other.
y-m-41-04.s.s2.because.hint.1: Pick one (u, v) from the cases that fix the prices and write how its ratio differs from Monday's record.
y-m-41-04.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you compare the ratios of Monday's record and Wednesday's record with numbers?
y-m-41-04.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you give the reason not as 'how many equations there are' but as 'whether there is new information'?
y-m-41-04.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Did you give one example of a case that does not fix the prices, with numbers?
y-m-41-04.s.s2.because.model.0: (1, 1) has a different ratio from Monday's (2, 3), so it becomes a new equation. On the other hand, a case like (4, 6), which is a multiple of Monday's, repeats the same information, so the prices are not fixed.
y-m-41-04.s.s2.because.model.1: If the ratio of the numbers sold on Wednesday is the same as Monday's 2 : 3, the two equations are effectively the same equation and there is no new information, and if the ratio is different, they are different equations, so x and y are fixed to one value.

y-m-41-05.title: What shape will come out if we keep taking powers?
y-m-41-05.topic: Repeating shapes in powers of a matrix and the range over which a rule can be generalized
y-m-41-05.goal: Predict a rule in powers of a matrix, revise the prediction and the degree of confidence according to new calculation results, and judge whether a rule found for one matrix may be carried over to another matrix.
y-m-41-05.material: A is a 2×2 matrix whose first row is (0, −1) and second row is (1, 0). E is the identity matrix (first row (1, 0), second row (0, 1)), and −E is the matrix with the signs of all entries changed. A² is A multiplied twice (A squared), and A³ is A multiplied three times. As data is revealed one piece at a time, revise your thinking about what shape will come out if we keep taking powers.
y-m-41-05.thinking.0: Predict the next result using a result already found
y-m-41-05.thinking.1: Revise judgments and confidence according to new data
y-m-41-05.thinking.2: Examine whether a rule from one example may be extended to all cases
y-m-41-05.prereq.0: The H1 label is only a difficulty and support tier for this production assignment, not a grade set by the curriculum. It assumes students who have already studied matrices at an introductory high school level.
y-m-41-05.prereq.1: You can calculate the product of 2×2 matrices and know the associative law of multiplication ((AB)C=A(BC))
y-m-41-05.prereq.2: Know the identity matrix E and the meaning of the powers A² and A³
y-m-41-05.s.s1.prompt: Choose a prediction each time data is revealed. After seeing new data, you may revise your thinking.
y-m-41-05.s.s1.hint.0: Try to see whether you can use the powers you already found again to get the next power.
y-m-41-05.s.s1.hint.1: Write A, A², A³, A⁴ in order in a table and look for places where the same shape appears again.
y-m-41-05.s.s1.st.0.info: When A² was calculated, it became −E (first row (−1, 0), second row (0, −1)), which has entries only on the diagonal.
y-m-41-05.s.s1.st.0.ask: What will A³ and A⁴ be? Choose the most suitable prediction from the data so far.
y-m-41-05.s.s1.st.0.after: A³=A²A=(−E)A=−A and A⁴=A²A²=(−E)(−E)=E. If you reuse a result you already found, you can predict without multiplying directly, and you can check this prediction by multiplying.
y-m-41-05.s.s1.st.0.o.a: The entries keep growing, so the entries of A⁴ will have a much larger absolute value than those of A²
y-m-41-05.s.s1.st.0.r.a: How the size of the entries changes comes from the structure of the product. Work out how the fact that A² is −E affects the later products.
y-m-41-05.s.s1.st.0.o.b: A³=−A and A⁴=E. You can just reuse the A² you already found
y-m-41-05.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You predicted without multiplying directly, by reusing a result you found.
y-m-41-05.s.s1.st.0.o.c: A³ is also −E and A⁴ is also −E, so it will keep being −E
y-m-41-05.s.s1.st.0.r.c: It seems you thought that because A² was −E, later ones are the same value. Check what you get when you multiply (−E) by A or by (−E).
y-m-41-05.s.s1.st.0.o.d: You cannot say anything about A³ before multiplying directly
y-m-41-05.s.s1.st.0.r.d: Look at whether you can use the A² you already know. There may be things you can know without multiplying anew.
y-m-41-05.s.s1.st.1.info: I checked by multiplying directly. A³ has first row (0, 1) and second row (−1, 0), and A⁴=E.
y-m-41-05.s.s1.st.1.ask: Then what matrix is A²⁰²⁶ (A to the power 2026), A multiplied 2026 times?
y-m-41-05.s.s1.st.1.after: Since A⁴=E, it returns to E every time A is multiplied four times. 2026 times is 506 groups of four with two left over, so A²⁰²⁶=A²=−E. This is because you may group the products using the associative law.
y-m-41-05.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You used the structure that it returns to E every four times and worked out the remaining count.
y-m-41-05.s.s1.st.1.r.b: It seems you thought it is E because 2026 is even. A² was −E. Not every even power is E.
y-m-41-05.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You may have thought so because A has its original form. First check at which multiplication it returns to E while multiplying 2026 times.
y-m-41-05.s.s1.st.1.o.d: Cannot tell. You have to multiply all 2026 times
y-m-41-05.s.s1.st.1.r.d: Using the result A⁴=E, you do not have to multiply 2026 times one by one. Look at how many multiplications it takes for the pattern to repeat.
y-m-41-05.s.s1.st.2.info: A friend says, "If you multiply a 2×2 matrix enough times, it will eventually return to E." You multiplied another matrix C (first row (2, 0), second row (0, 1)): C² has first row (4, 0) and second row (0, 1), and C³ has first row (8, 0) and second row (0, 1).
y-m-41-05.s.s1.st.2.ask: How do you judge the friend's statement?
y-m-41-05.s.s1.st.2.after: The entry at row 1, column 1 of C is 2, 4, 8, doubling each time (the form 2 to the n-th power). If this rule continues, C does not return to E. 'A repeats every four times' is a fact about A, not a property of all matrices. How much you trust a rule depends on the evidence (whether you checked it directly).
y-m-41-05.s.s1.st.2.o.a: A returned to E, so C will eventually become E if multiplied a few more times
y-m-41-05.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You carried the rule of one matrix over to another matrix. Look at how the entries at row 1, column 1 of C² and C³ change.
y-m-41-05.s.s1.st.2.o.b: A returning to E was a coincidence, so the result for A cannot be trusted either
y-m-41-05.s.s1.st.2.r.b: A⁴=E is a result checked by multiplying directly. Tell apart what was confirmed for one matrix from generalizing to all matrices.
y-m-41-05.s.s1.st.2.o.c: C does not seem to return to E, so the friend's statement is hard to believe
y-m-41-05.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You did not use the rule found for one matrix as it is for another matrix, and weighed it with the new data.
y-m-41-05.s.s1.st.2.o.d: You have only seen C three times, so you cannot make any judgment
y-m-41-05.s.s1.st.2.r.d: In the results of the three times, you can see a regular change in which row 1, column 1 doubles. Think about what you can say from that change.
y-m-41-05.s.s1.reflect: How did your confidence change when you knew only A², when you knew up to A⁴, and after you saw C? When can you trust a repeating rule, and when do you need to check more?
y-m-41-05.s.s2.prompt: Write a reply to the friend's statement. In one or two sentences, write how you found A²⁰²⁶ and why that method cannot be used for C as it is.
y-m-41-05.s.s2.hint.0: First write the method you used to find A²⁰²⁶ in one sentence, and for C write what you can tell from looking at C² and C³.
y-m-41-05.s.s2.hint.1: Compare which of the A case and the C case has the same rule repeating.
y-m-41-05.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you start from the confirmed fact A⁴=E?
y-m-41-05.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you mention the remaining count (what is left when you group 2026 by fours)?
y-m-41-05.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you explain the difference between C and A with numbers (2, 4, 8, and so on)?
y-m-41-05.s.s2.model.0: If you multiply A four times it returns to E, so if you group 2026 times by fours, two are left over, and A²=−E. For C, the entry at row 1, column 1 just keeps getting larger as you multiply and it never returns to E, so you cannot use this method.
y-m-41-05.s.s2.model.1: Because A⁴=E, I used the fact that the cycle in which the same shape repeats is 4. C keeps growing like 2, 4, 8 and does not repeat, so this method does not work.
y-m-41-05.s.s2.model.2: Since the remainder when 2026 is divided by 4 is 2, A²⁰²⁶ equals A². C keeps getting bigger and never becomes E, so the friend's statement is wrong.

y-m-41-06.title: Two friends who disagree about the inverse matrix of AB
y-m-41-06.topic: The inverse matrix of a product of two matrices: the order of multiplying inverse matrices
y-m-41-06.goal: Compare two candidate formulas using one example, tell apart what one example can and cannot show, and then explain with letters the order of multiplying inverse matrices for general matrices.
y-m-41-06.material: A has first row (1, 2) and second row (0, 1), and B has first row (1, 0) and second row (3, 1). Both have inverse matrices. The inverse matrix of A has first row (1, −2) and second row (0, 1), and the inverse matrix of B has first row (1, 0) and second row (−3, 1). The product AB has first row (7, 2) and second row (3, 1). Haeun says, "The inverse matrix of AB is the inverse matrix of A followed by the inverse matrix of B," and Doyun says, "You have to multiply the inverse matrix of B followed by the inverse matrix of A." Call the matrix calculated by Haeun's formula X (first row (7, −2), second row (−3, 1)), and the matrix calculated by Doyun's formula Y (first row (1, −2), second row (−3, 7)).
y-m-41-06.thinking.0: Test the candidates by calculation and compare them
y-m-41-06.thinking.1: Tell apart what one example can deny and what it cannot settle
y-m-41-06.thinking.2: Build a general argument with letters
y-m-41-06.prereq.0: The H1 label is only a difficulty and support tier for this production assignment, not a grade set by the curriculum. It assumes students who have already studied matrices at an introductory high school level.
y-m-41-06.prereq.1: You can calculate the product of 2×2 matrices and know the associative law of multiplication ((AB)C=A(BC))
y-m-41-06.prereq.2: Know the meaning of an inverse matrix (a matrix that gives the identity matrix E when multiplied)
y-m-41-06.s.s1.prompt: Check by multiplying AB by X and by Y. What is the inverse matrix of AB?
y-m-41-06.s.s1.hint.0: Calculate the matrix of AB times X and the matrix of AB times Y.
y-m-41-06.s.s1.hint.1: Compare, entry by entry, whether the results you calculated equal the identity matrix (first row (1, 0), second row (0, 1)).
y-m-41-06.s.s1.o.b: Both X and Y are inverse matrices of AB
y-m-41-06.s.s1.r.b: An inverse matrix is a matrix that gives the identity matrix when multiplied, and there is only one. First compare whether X and Y are the same matrix.
y-m-41-06.s.s1.o.d: Neither X nor Y is the inverse matrix of AB
y-m-41-06.s.s1.r.d: If one of them is right but you said neither, there may be an entry where the calculation went off. Recalculate the two products.
y-m-41-06.s.s1.explain: (AB)Y has first row (1, 0) and second row (0, 1), so it is the identity matrix, but (AB)X is not the identity matrix. So in this example the inverse matrix of AB is Y.
y-m-41-06.s.s2.prompt: What can you say from the result of this one example?
y-m-41-06.s.s2.hint.0: In this example, first check whether the matrix obtained by Haeun's formula became the inverse matrix.
y-m-41-06.s.s2.hint.1: Work out whether the fact that Doyun's formula was right is evidence that it is right for all A and B.
y-m-41-06.s.s2.o.c: Both formulas are sometimes right and sometimes wrong, so the only way is to calculate directly and check each time
y-m-41-06.s.s2.r.c: This example showed that Haeun's formula can be wrong. But a case where Doyun's formula is wrong has not been shown yet.
y-m-41-06.s.s2.o.d: X and Y are actually the same matrix, so you do not need to care about the order of multiplying
y-m-41-06.s.s2.r.d: Compare the entries at row 1, column 1 of X and Y. First check whether they are the same matrix.
y-m-41-06.s.s2.explain: Haeun's formula did not give the inverse matrix of AB in this example, so it is not an always-right formula (a counterexample). But the fact that Doyun's formula was right in this example alone does not let us say it is right for all A and B, so it must be checked separately with letters.
y-m-41-06.s.s3.prompt: When A and B are general matrices with inverse matrices, in what order must you multiply the inverse matrix of A and the inverse matrix of B to make the inverse matrix of AB? Show the reason with letters.
y-m-41-06.s.s3.hint.0: Write with symbols the expression where a candidate matrix is multiplied on the right of AB, and find the two matrices that meet in the middle.
y-m-41-06.s.s3.hint.1: Compare which matrix must meet first in the middle for (AB)(candidate) to become E.
y-m-41-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you compute the product of AB and the candidate matrix with symbols alone and show the process by which the identity matrix comes out?
y-m-41-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you give a general reason, not that it was right in one example?
y-m-41-06.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you explain why the order of multiplying is opposite to A, B?
y-m-41-06.s.s3.model.0: (AB)(B⁻¹A⁻¹)=A(BB⁻¹)A⁻¹=AEA⁻¹=AA⁻¹=E, so B⁻¹A⁻¹ is the inverse matrix of AB. For B and B⁻¹ to meet first on the inside and vanish, the order has to be reversed.
y-m-41-06.s.s3.model.1: If you multiply the inverse matrix of B on the right of AB, B vanishes, and if you then multiply the inverse matrix of A, A vanishes and the identity matrix remains. So the order must be the inverse matrix of B first and the inverse matrix of A later.
y-m-41-06.s.s1.o.a: Only Y is the inverse matrix of AB
y-m-41-06.s.s1.r.a: This is a judgment that uses evidence from multiplying the candidate directly and checking whether it gives the identity matrix.
y-m-41-06.s.s1.o.c: Only X is the inverse matrix of AB
y-m-41-06.s.s1.r.c: Look back at whether you checked all four entries to the end when X is multiplied by AB to see if it gives the identity matrix.
y-m-41-06.s.s2.o.a: Doyun's formula is always right. This is because it was right in this example
y-m-41-06.s.s2.r.a: One example being right does not mean it is right in every case. Think about how to check whether there are cases where Doyun's formula can be wrong.
y-m-41-06.s.s2.o.b: Haeun's formula is not always right. Whether Doyun's formula is always right has to be checked separately with letters
y-m-41-06.s.s2.r.b: It distinguished what one example can deny from what it cannot confirm.
y-m-41-06.s.s3.model.2: An inverse matrix is a matrix that gives the identity matrix E when multiplied. For the inverse of AB, you must multiply the inverse of B and then the inverse of A, so that the middle parts meet each other and vanish.

y-m-41-07.title: If we square each entry, does it become the square of the matrix?
y-m-41-07.topic: Finding cases where the misconception of computing a matrix square by squaring entries holds
y-m-41-07.goal: Find the matrices for which the misconception 'the square of a matrix is each entry squared' holds, work out the condition, and also judge that this range does not carry over to powers in general.
y-m-41-07.material: Minseo said, "The square of a matrix A equals the matrix with each entry squared separately." A is a 2×2 matrix whose first row is (a, b) and second row is (c, d), and call the matrix with each entry squared separately A* (first row (a², b²), second row (c², d²), read as 'a squared'). A² is the matrix product A×A. For example, if the first row of A is (1, 2) and the second row is (3, 4), A² has first row (7, 10) and second row (15, 22), and A* has first row (1, 4) and second row (9, 16). All the entries are integers.
y-m-41-07.thinking.0: Find cases where the misconception holds by working with letters
y-m-41-07.thinking.1: Make different examples that satisfy the condition
y-m-41-07.thinking.2: Check whether a property that held once also holds for the next power
y-m-41-07.prereq.0: The H1 label is only a difficulty and support tier for this production assignment, not a grade set by the curriculum. It assumes students who have already studied matrices at an introductory high school level.
y-m-41-07.prereq.1: You can calculate the product of 2×2 matrices using entries
y-m-41-07.s.s1.prompt: In the example above, A² and A* were different. Then what is the most suitable first step to find out whether there is a matrix with A²=A*?
y-m-41-07.s.s1.hint.0: Write the entry at row 1, column 1 of A² directly in terms of a, b, c, and compare it with the entry at the same position of A*.
y-m-41-07.s.s1.hint.1: Write down one by one what condition is needed to make the same formula come out at all four positions.
y-m-41-07.s.s1.o.a: Since they were different in the example, decide that there is no matrix with A²=A*
y-m-41-07.s.s1.r.a: Being different for one matrix does not mean being different for every matrix. Think about a way to find whether there are matrices where they are equal.
y-m-41-07.s.s1.o.b: Write the four entries of A² with letters and compare them with the entries at the same positions of A*
y-m-41-07.s.s1.r.b: You set up the condition with a letter formula that can handle all cases at once, going beyond an example.
y-m-41-07.s.s1.o.c: Decide in advance that it holds only for diagonal matrices (b and c both 0), and test only that
y-m-41-07.s.s1.r.c: You narrowed the range in advance. Keep open whether there are cases where they are equal even for matrices that are not diagonal, and test it.
y-m-41-07.s.s1.o.d: Put various numbers into A and look for cases where A² and A* are equal
y-m-41-07.s.s1.r.d: Trying various numbers is also a good way to explore. After you find one, check with letters why that condition is needed.
y-m-41-07.s.s1.explain: Writing the four entries of A² with letters gives first row (a²+bc, ab+bd) and second row (ca+dc, cb+d²). Comparing with A* at the same positions, the conditions are bc=0, b(a+d)=b², c(a+d)=c². Exploring by putting in numbers is also good, but a letter formula shows all cases at once.
y-m-41-07.s.s1.acc.0: Exploring by putting in various numbers is also a reasonable start. But why the example you found works has to be checked with a letter formula.
y-m-41-07.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different A with A²=A* that are not diagonal matrices (at least one of b and c is not 0). The entries a, b, c, d are integers from −9 to 9.
y-m-41-07.s.s2.hint.0: Write the four entries of A² and the four entries of A* with letters, and write the equations that set the same positions equal.
y-m-41-07.s.s2.hint.1: To make bc equal 0, set one of b and c to 0, and find values that satisfy the remaining equations.
y-m-41-07.s.s2.ok.c1: The entries are integers from −9 to 9.
y-m-41-07.s.s2.fail.c1: The entries must be integers from −9 to 9.
y-m-41-07.s.s2.ok.c2: Row 1, column 1 and row 2, column 2 of A² equal a² and d².
y-m-41-07.s.s2.fail.c2: Row 1, column 1 of A² (a²+bc) does not equal a².
y-m-41-07.s.s2.ok.c3: Row 1, column 2 of A² equals b².
y-m-41-07.s.s2.fail.c3: Row 1, column 2 of A² (ab+bd) does not equal b².
y-m-41-07.s.s2.ok.c4: Row 2, column 1 of A² equals c².
y-m-41-07.s.s2.fail.c4: Row 2, column 1 of A² (ca+dc) does not equal c².
y-m-41-07.s.s2.ok.c5: It is not a diagonal matrix.
y-m-41-07.s.s2.fail.c5: It is a diagonal matrix with b and c both 0. You need to find an example that is not a diagonal matrix.
y-m-41-07.s.s2.explain: The conditions are bc=0, b(a+d)=b², c(a+d)=c². If b≠0 then c=0 and a+d=b must hold, and if c≠0 then b=0 and a+d=c must hold. For example, with first row (1, 3) and second row (0, 2), A² has first row (1, 9) and second row (0, 4), and A* is the same.
y-m-41-07.s.s2.because.prompt: With one A you found, calculate one entry of A² directly and show it equals the entry at the same position of A*, and write how you found such an A.
y-m-41-07.s.s2.because.hint.0: Put the entries of the A you chose into row 1, column 2 of A² (or another entry), write it out as products and sums, and compare it with the same position of A*.
y-m-41-07.s.s2.because.hint.1: Check whether you repeated the same rule (which entry you set to 0) when making several A.
y-m-41-07.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: With the A you chose, did you work out one entry of A² by writing it as products and sums?
y-m-41-07.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you compare the value with the entry at the same position of A*?
y-m-41-07.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Did you describe how you searched, such as setting one of b and c to 0 or matching a+d?
y-m-41-07.s.s2.because.model.0: If the first row of A is (1, 3) and the second row is (0, 2), row 1, column 2 of A² is 1×3+3×2=9, and row 1, column 2 of A* is 3²=9, which is equal. I set c to 0 and chose values so that a+d equals b.
y-m-41-07.s.s2.because.model.1: If the first row of A is (4, 0) and the second row is (5, 1), row 2, column 1 of A² is 5×4+1×5=25, and row 2, column 1 of A* is 5²=25. I set b to 0 and chose values so that a+d equals c.
y-m-41-07.s.s3.prompt: Among the A you found, look at the A whose first row is (1, 3) and second row is (0, 2). The A² of this A has first row (1, 9) and second row (0, 4), equal to A*. Then are A³ (=A²×A) and the matrix with each entry cubed separately (row 1, column 2 is 3³=27) also equal? Judge by calculating row 1, column 2 of A³ directly.
y-m-41-07.s.s3.hint.0: Using A³=A²×A, write which sum of two products the entry at row 1, column 2 of A³ is.
y-m-41-07.s.s3.hint.1: Compare the value you got with the cube of 3, and if even one position differs, work out whether the two matrices are equal.
y-m-41-07.s.s3.o.a: Row 1, column 2 of A³ is 27. So A³ also equals the entrywise cube
y-m-41-07.s.s3.r.a: 27 is 3³, not an entry of A³. Row 1, column 2 of A³ has to be calculated by the definition of the product.
y-m-41-07.s.s3.o.b: Row 1, column 2 of A³ is 21. Still, the other entries are equal, so A³ equals the entrywise cube
y-m-41-07.s.s3.r.b: For matrices to be equal, the entries at all positions must be equal. If even one position differs, they are not the same matrix.
y-m-41-07.s.s3.o.c: Row 1, column 2 of A³ is 18. So A³ differs from the entrywise cube
y-m-41-07.s.s3.r.c: The conclusion is the same, but 18 is a value in which some terms are missing from the calculation. Check whether you also added the product of row 1, column 1 of A² and row 1, column 2 of A.
y-m-41-07.s.s3.o.d: Row 1, column 2 of A³ is 21. So A³ differs from the entrywise cube
y-m-41-07.s.s3.r.d: You checked by direct calculation whether a property that held for A² also holds for A³.
y-m-41-07.s.s3.explain: Row 1, column 2 of A³=A²×A is 1×3+9×2=21. Row 1, column 2 of the entrywise cube is 3³=27, so the two matrices are different. Even if A²=A* holds, it may not hold for A³, so you must not believe that a property keeps holding just because it held once.

y-m-41-08.title: A product that can be calculated and a product that has meaning
y-m-41-08.topic: The quantity an entry of a matrix product stands for and the meaning of the order of multiplying
y-m-41-08.goal: Know that a matrix product being calculable is different from its entries having meaning, and judge the order of multiplying by matching what the rows and columns refer to.
y-m-41-08.material: Two stores (가, 나) sell bread and milk. N is the matrix of daily sales counts, with rows as stores (가, 나) and columns as products (bread, milk). Store 가 sells 3 breads and 2 milks, and store 나 sells 1 bread and 4 milks, so the first row of N is (3, 2) and the second row is (1, 4). Q is the matrix of price per item (원), with rows as products (bread, milk) and columns as seasons (summer, winter). Bread is 1000원 in summer and 1100원 in winter, and milk is 800원 in summer and 900원 in winter, so the first row of Q is (1000, 1100) and the second row is (800, 900). Both matrices are 2×2, so both NQ and QN can be calculated. NQ has first row (4600, 5100) and second row (4200, 4700), and QN has first row (4100, 6400) and second row (3300, 5200).

y-m-41-09.title: If an entry is 0, is there no inverse matrix?
y-m-41-09.topic: The condition for a 2×2 matrix to have an inverse matrix and its relation to whether an entry is 0
y-m-41-09.goal: Test two friends' opposite claims each with a counterexample, learn that whether an entry is 0 does not decide whether an inverse matrix exists, and design directly a matrix that has no inverse matrix.
y-m-41-09.material: Let the first row of a 2×2 matrix M be (a, b) and the second row be (c, d). A necessary and sufficient condition for M to have an inverse matrix is that ad−bc is not 0 (in this task we use this condition without proving it). The entries a, b, c, d are all integers. Two friends said this. Soyun: "If even one entry is 0, there is no inverse matrix." Dohyeon: "If no entry is 0, there is an inverse matrix."
y-m-41-09.thinking.0: Test the friends' claims by making counterexamples
y-m-41-09.thinking.1: Tell apart the outward look of the entries from whether an inverse matrix exists
y-m-41-09.thinking.2: Design different examples that fit a condition
y-m-41-09.prereq.0: The H1 label is only a difficulty and support tier for this production assignment, not a grade set by the curriculum. It assumes students who have already studied matrices at an introductory high school level.
y-m-41-09.prereq.1: You have learned the condition for a 2×2 matrix to have an inverse matrix (in this task that condition is given in the material below)
y-m-41-09.prereq.2: You can refer to the entries of a 2×2 matrix by position (row 1, column 2, and so on)
y-m-41-09.s.s1.prompt: How do you judge the two friends' statements? Choose your thinking before making examples and testing.
y-m-41-09.s.s1.hint.0: Write in a sentence what kind of matrix must exist for Soyun's statement to be wrong.
y-m-41-09.s.s1.hint.1: Starting with the simplest matrices (for example, ones with only 0 and 1 as entries), calculate the value of ad−bc.
y-m-41-09.s.s1.o.a: Only Soyun's statement is right. If there is a 0, one of ad or bc becomes 0 and ad−bc also becomes 0
y-m-41-09.s.s1.r.a: Even if one product is 0, if the other product is not 0, ad−bc may not be 0. Test what the difference of the two products turns out to be.
y-m-41-09.s.s1.o.b: Only Dohyeon's statement is right. If no entry is 0, ad and bc are both not 0, so ad−bc is also not 0
y-m-41-09.s.s1.r.b: Even if ad and bc are both not 0, if the two values are equal, the difference is 0. Test whether there are cases where the two products are equal.
y-m-41-09.s.s1.o.c: Both are right. Whether an inverse matrix exists is decided by whether there is a 0 among the entries
y-m-41-09.s.s1.r.c: Whether an inverse matrix exists is decided by the value of ad−bc. Test using that value as the criterion, not the outward look of the entries.
y-m-41-09.s.s1.o.d: Neither is right. For each statement there is an example that breaks it
y-m-41-09.s.s1.r.d: You thought in the direction of checking separately whether there is a counterexample for each claim.
y-m-41-09.s.s1.explain: Soyun's statement is wrong if there is even one 'matrix that has a 0 yet has an inverse matrix', and Dohyeon's statement is wrong if there is even one 'matrix whose entries are all non-zero yet has no inverse matrix'. Both counterexamples exist, so neither statement is right.
y-m-41-09.s.s2.prompt: Make two different matrices that break Soyun's statement, that is, matrices that have a 0 among the entries and also have an inverse matrix. The entries a, b, c, d are integers from −9 to 9.
y-m-41-09.s.s2.hint.0: Set only one entry to 0 and the rest to non-zero values, and calculate ad−bc.
y-m-41-09.s.s2.hint.1: If ad−bc turns out to be 0, change the position of the 0 or the other entries.
y-m-41-09.s.s2.ok.c1: The entries are integers from −9 to 9.
y-m-41-09.s.s2.fail.c1: The entries must be integers from −9 to 9.
y-m-41-09.s.s2.ok.c2: There is a 0 among the entries.
y-m-41-09.s.s2.fail.c2: There is no 0 at all among the entries.
y-m-41-09.s.s2.ok.c3: ad−bc is not 0, so there is an inverse matrix.
y-m-41-09.s.s2.fail.c3: ad−bc is 0, so there is no inverse matrix.
y-m-41-09.s.s2.explain: For example, first row (2, 3) and second row (0, 5) has a 0 among the entries but ad−bc=10, so it has an inverse matrix. The criterion is not whether there is a 0 but whether the difference of ad and bc is 0. A matrix like (0, 0, 1, 1) that has a 0 and has no inverse matrix is just a case where Soyun's statement is right, so it is not a counterexample.
